summary:
Exploring Mixtures and their Separation (Grade 9 Chemistry - Complete Chapter 5, Pages 73-93):

1. Classification of Mixtures (Section 5.1):
• Homogeneous Mixtures (Solutions): Uniform composition throughout; components do not settle; no visible separation boundaries (e.g., sugar syrup, common salt in water, vinegar, aerated soda, air, brass). Always remains homogeneous.
• Heterogeneous Mixtures: Non-uniform composition with physically distinct boundaries (e.g., sand in water, chalk in water, oil and water, muddy water, milk, blood, smoke, fog).
• Activity 5.1 Observations:
  - Salt + Water: True solution; particles invisible, transparent, does not scatter laser light, stable without settling, leaves no residue upon filtration.
  - Chalk + Water: Suspension; particles visible, scatters laser light, unstable (particles settle), leaves chalk residue on filter paper.
  - Milk + Water: Colloid; particles not individually visible, distinctly scatters laser beam (Tyndall effect), stable, passes through filter paper without residue.
  - Safety Warning: Never look directly into a laser beam as it can cause irreversible eye damage.

2. Solutions and Concentration (Sections 5.2 & 5.2.1):
• Solution = Solute (dissolved substance, smaller proportion) + Solvent (dissolving medium, larger proportion).
• Concentration: The amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent or total solution.
• Life-Saving Milestone (Meet a Scientist): Dr. Dilip Mahalanabis formulated Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) containing precise ratios of salt and sugar in water to treat dehydration caused by cholera and diarrhoea, saving millions of lives worldwide under WHO guidance. Arbitrary sugary drinks do NOT constitute ORS.
• Agricultural & Everyday Importance: Farmers must maintain exact pesticide concentrations; improper concentrations harm crops and soil. Concentration is vital in foods, cosmetics, medicines, and labs.

3. Methods to Express Concentration (Section 5.2.2):
• Mass by Mass (% m/m or % w/w): [Mass of solute / Mass of solution] × 100. Mass of solution = Mass of solute + Mass of solvent. Used for milk powder, spice blends, and food nutrition labels.
  - Example 5.1: 10 g salt in 90 g water = 10% m/m.
  - Pause & Ponder 1: 4% m/m zinc oxide (antiseptic) in 300 g talcum powder = 12 g zinc oxide.
  - Cake Recipe (Q4): 75 g sugar (15% m/m), 420 g flour (84% m/m), 5 g baking soda (1% m/m) in 500 g total dry mix.
  - Brass Alloy (Q4): 70% copper in 120 g brass = 84 g copper and 36 g zinc.
  - Sugar Solutions (Q14): Student A (20% m/m), Student B (16.67% m/m), Student C (27.27% m/m - most concentrated).
• Mass by Volume (% m/v or % w/v): [Mass of solute (g) / Volume of solution (mL)] × 100. Preferred in medicines and laboratories where measuring liquid volume is easier than weighing.
  - Example 5.2: 5 g glucose in 100 mL solution = 5% m/v.
  - Saline Drip (Threads of Curiosity): Standard hospital IV drip contains 0.9% m/v sodium chloride, matching human blood plasma osmolarity.
• Volume by Volume (% v/v): [Volume of solute (mL) / Volume of solution (mL)] × 100. Used for miscible liquids (perfumes, cosmetics, vinegar).
  - Example 5.3: 1 mL liquid pesticide in 100 mL spray = 1% v/v.
  - Pause & Ponder 2: 2 tablespoons (30 mL) orange concentrate diluted to 150 mL juice = 20% v/v.
  - Pause & Ponder 3: To make 5% v/v vinegar from 100% glacial acetic acid, dilute 5 mL glacial acetic acid with water up to 100 mL.

4. Solubility and Solubility Data Analysis (Section 5.2.3, Table 5.4):
• Solubility: Maximum mass of solute (in grams) dissolved in 100 g of solvent at a specific temperature to form a saturated solution.
• Temperature Effect: Increases for most solid solutes in liquids; decreases for gases in liquids.
• Quantitative Salt Analysis (Table 5.4):
  - Potassium nitrate (KNO3): Solubility surges from 21 g at 10 °C to 167 g at 80 °C (+146 g increase, highest temperature sensitivity). At 40 °C, 50 g water requires exactly 31 g KNO3 to saturate.
  - Sodium chloride (NaCl): Solubility rises negligibly from 36 g at 10 °C to 37 g at 80 °C (+1 g, least temperature-sensitive).
  - Potassium chloride (KCl): Solubility increases from 35 g at 10 °C to 54 g at 80 °C. Cooling saturated KCl from 80 °C to 25 °C deposits solid KCl crystals.
  - Ammonium chloride (NH4Cl): Increases from 24 g at 10 °C to 66 g at 80 °C (+42 g).

5. Crystallization (Section 5.3.1, Pages 77-79):
• Crystal: A pure solid substance composed of particles arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional geometric lattice.
• Everyday & Natural Crystals: Rock salt, candy sugar (mishri), snowflakes, window frost, Mawsmai Cave in Sohra (Cherrapunji), and quartz.
• Activity 5.3 (Copper Sulfate Crystallization):
  - Add 1 drop of dilute sulfuric acid to prevent hydrolysis and unwanted reactions.
  - Prepare hot saturated solution in a water bath, filter hot to remove insoluble impurities.
  - Cool slowly and undisturbed to allow particles ample time to assemble into large, shiny, well-formed blue crystals.
• Scientific Inquiry (Think as a Scientist):
  - Rapid cooling in ice-cold water produces tiny, poorly-formed crystals.
  - Slow cooling at room temperature produces large, well-defined crystals.
• Pause & Ponder 5: Slow evaporation of salt water yields larger crystals; rapid evaporation yields smaller crystals.
• Traditional Indian Salt Production: Panga salt (boiling sea brines) and Karkatch salt (solar evaporation of sea water).
• Separation by Crystallization: Saturated solution of Compound B cooled from 60 °C (287 g) to 40 °C (241 g) deposits 46 g of pure crystals per 100 g water.

6. Distillation (Section 5.3.2, Pages 80-81, 93):
• Definition: Separation of two miscible liquids by vaporizing the lower-boiling liquid and condensing its vapours: Liquid -> Vapour -> Liquid (Distillate).
• Criteria: Boiling point difference must be at least 25 °C (or 25 K).
• Apparatus (Fig. 5.26): Distillation flask (A), Liebig water condenser (B, water inlet at bottom, outlet at top), and receiving conical flask (C).
• Feasibility on Table 5.5 Compounds:
  - Water (100 °C) - Acetone (56 °C): Δ = 44 °C (≥ 25 °C) -> Separated by simple distillation.
  - Water (100 °C) - Salt: Volatile liquid and non-volatile solid -> Separated by distillation.
  - Acetone (56 °C) - Alcohol (78 °C): Δ = 22 °C (< 25 °C) -> Requires fractional distillation.
  - Alcohol (78 °C) - Chloroform (61 °C): Δ = 17 °C (< 25 °C) -> Requires fractional distillation.
  - Alcohol (78 °C) - Benzene (80 °C): Δ = 2 °C (< 25 °C) -> Requires fractional distillation.
• India's Scientific Heritage (Kannauj Perfumery):
  - Kannauj in Uttar Pradesh is the "Perfume Capital of India".
  - Traditional Deg-Bhapka distillation method produces Mitti ka Ittar (earthy fragrance of rain on soil).
  - Supported by the Fragrance and Flavour Development Centre (FFDC).
• Fractional Distillation: Used when boiling point differences are less than 25 °C. Refines crude petroleum into LPG, petrol, kerosene/aviation fuel, diesel, lubricating oil, and bitumen.

7. Paper Chromatography (Section 5.3.3, Page 82):
• Origin: Greek chroma ('colour') + graphein ('to write') = 'writing with colour'.
• Principle: Separates components based on relative solubility in mobile phase and affinity for stationary paper phase.
• Activity 5.5: Pencil line 2 cm from bottom of filter paper; black ink spot placed; paper dipped in water ensuring solvent level is BELOW the spot. Coloured dyes rise at different speeds, separating into bands.
• Investigating Red Leaves: Chromatography reveals that red leaves also contain green chlorophyll, masked by red anthocyanins.

8. Heterogeneous Mixtures Separation (Section 5.4, Pages 83-86, 92):
• Separating Funnel (5.4.1): Separates immiscible liquids based on density differences (e.g., cooking oil [density 0.91 g/mL] floats on water [density 1.0 g/mL]; water drained first via stopcock).
• Sublimation (5.4.2): Direct transition from solid to gas on heating; reverse is deposition. Separates camphor, naphthalene, ammonium chloride, and dry ice (solid CO2) from non-sublimable solids like sand.
• Multicomponent Separation (Sand, Salt, Naphthalene - Q11):
  Step 1: Sublimation to separate naphthalene.
  Step 2: Dissolution in water to dissolve salt.
  Step 3: Filtration to remove insoluble sand.
  Step 4: Evaporation / Crystallization to recover pure salt crystals.
• Alloys: Homogeneous mixtures of metals/non-metals that cannot be separated by physical methods (Brass: Cu 70-80%, Zn 20-30%; Bronze: Cu 80%, Sn 20%; Stainless Steel: Fe + C, Cr 16-18%, Ni 10-14%, Mo 2-3%).
• Suspensions & Centrifugation (5.4.3): Heterogeneous non-settling suspensions separated by spinning at high speed (centrifugal force pushes denser particles outward/downward). Analogy: Phugadi/Kikli folk spinning. Clinical use: blood plasma separation. Innovation: The Paperfuge (low-cost whirligig centrifuge diagnosing malaria/anaemia in remote clinics without power).
• Coagulation: Powdered alum (fitkari) neutralizes charges on fine suspended clay particles in muddy water, causing them to clump into heavy flocs that settle by gravity (sedimentation), followed by decantation. Culinary use: making paneer (cheese) using lemon juice/vinegar.

9. Colloids, Emulsions & Tyndall Effect (Sections 5.4.4 & 5.5, Pages 86-88):
• Particle Size Spectrum:
  - True Solution: < 1 nm (invisible, no Tyndall effect, does not settle).
  - Colloid: 1 nm to 1000 nm (invisible to naked eye, exhibits Tyndall effect, stable without settling).
  - Suspension: > 1000 nm (visible to naked eye, exhibits Tyndall effect, settles on standing).
• Components of Colloid: Dispersed Phase (solute-like particles) and Dispersion Medium (continuous medium). In blood, cells are dispersed phase and plasma is dispersion medium.
• Emulsions: Liquid-in-liquid colloids. Oil-in-water (milk, vanishing cream) and Water-in-oil (butter, cold cream), stabilized by emulsifying agents (proteins in milk, soap).
• Tyndall Effect: Scattering of light beam by particles in a colloid or suspension (John Tyndall). Seen in dusty sunbeams, forest canopies, car fog lamps, and sports stadium floodlights. Clouds are aerosol colloids. City haze is caused by smoke/dust scattering light.

10. Environmental & Biological Separation (Pages 89-93):
• Kidneys remove urea/waste from blood. Sewage treatment uses sedimentation, coagulation, and filtration. Waste segregation divides Dry (recycling) and Wet (composting) wastes. Lithium is recycled from old phone and laptop batteries. The quest continues for artificial blood substitutes.

sa.q: Differentiate between a homogeneous mixture and a heterogeneous mixture with two examples of each.
sa.a: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout with no visible boundaries separating its components (e.g., sugar syrup, vinegar). A heterogeneous mixture has a non-uniform composition where constituent substances remain physically distinct with observable boundaries (e.g., sand in water, oil in water).

sa.q: Why does a laser beam pass invisibly through a salt solution but produce a visible illuminated beam through milk in water?
sa.a: Salt in water forms a true solution where dissolved solute particles are smaller than 1 nm, which cannot scatter visible light. Milk in water is a colloid containing suspended fat and protein particles (1–1000 nm) large enough to scatter light rays, producing the visible Tyndall effect.

sa.q: Name four major types of mixture separation techniques described in the chapter and state the physical property difference upon which each technique relies.
sa.a:
The four primary separation techniques are:
(i) Crystallization: Relies on the difference in solubility of a solid solute at varying temperatures to obtain pure crystals.
(ii) Distillation (Simple & Fractional): Relies on differences in boiling points between miscible liquids (Δb.p. ≥ 25 °C for simple distillation; < 25 °C for fractional distillation).
(iii) Separating Funnel: Relies on differences in density between two immiscible liquids.
(iv) Sublimation: Relies on the property of a sublimable solid changing directly into vapour on heating, separating it from non-sublimable solids.

sa.q: Why is distillation an effective method for separating a mixture of water and acetone, but ineffective for acetone and alcohol? (Exercise 12, Page 92)
sa.a: Water (100 °C) and acetone (56 °C) have a boiling point difference of 44 °C, well above the required 25 °C threshold. Volatile acetone boils first, vaporizes, and condenses into the receiver while water remains behind. Acetone (56 °C) and alcohol (78 °C) differ by only 22 °C (< 25 °C), so their vapours would distill together, requiring a fractionating column instead.

sa.q: Describe how a separating funnel is used to separate cooking oil from water, and state which liquid is drained first.
sa.a: Cooking oil and water are immiscible liquids. Cooking oil has a lower density (0.91 g/mL) and floats as the upper layer, while denser water (1.00 g/mL) settles as the lower layer. Opening the stopcock drains the denser water layer first into a receiving beaker. The stopcock is closed as soon as the interface reaches the bore, retaining the oil inside the funnel.

sa.q: State the principle of paper chromatography and explain why the reference baseline must be drawn with a pencil rather than a ballpoint pen.
sa.a: Paper chromatography separates components based on their differential solubility in a mobile solvent and differential affinity for stationary paper fibers. The baseline must be drawn with a pencil because insoluble graphite does not dissolve in the solvent, whereas pen ink contains soluble organic dyes that would dissolve, run, and obscure the chromatogram.

sa.q: A student makes a saturated solution of potassium chloride at 80 °C and lets it cool to room temperature (25 °C). What observation does she make, and why? (Exercise 13 ii)
sa.a: White solid crystals of potassium chloride separate out and deposit at the bottom of the beaker. This happens because the solubility of KCl decreases as the temperature drops (from 54 g at 80 °C to ~36 g at 25 °C); the cooler solvent cannot keep the excess solute dissolved, causing it to precipitate out as crystals.

sa.q: Explain the mechanism by which powdered alum (fitkari) purifies turbid muddy water.
sa.a: Colloidal clay particles suspended in muddy water carry identical negative electrical surface charges that keep them repelling each other and suspended. Powdered alum dissociates into trivalent aluminium ions (Al³⁺) that neutralize these negative surface charges. The neutralized clay particles collide, clump into heavy flocs (coagulation), and rapidly settle to the bottom by gravity (sedimentation).

sa.q: Explain the working principle of centrifugation and describe how the Paperfuge serves rural healthcare.
sa.a: Centrifugation spins mixtures at high rotational speeds, generating outward centrifugal force that drives denser suspended particles to the bottom of the tube while lighter liquid remains as a clear supernatant on top. The Paperfuge is a low-cost, electricity-free hand-powered centrifuge spinning at over 100,000 rpm, separating blood cells from plasma in 90 seconds to diagnose malaria and anaemia in remote non-electrified clinics.

sa.q: Outline the step-by-step sequence to separate a solid mixture of sand, common salt, and naphthalene (Exercise 11, Page 92).
sa.a:
The correct sequence is:
1. Step 1 (Sublimation - Fig. 5.25b Image 1): Heat the mixture under an inverted funnel; naphthalene sublimes directly into vapour and deposits on the cooler funnel walls.
2. Step 2 (Dissolution): Add water to the residual sand-salt mixture; salt dissolves completely, while sand remains undissolved.
3. Step 3 (Filtration - Fig. 5.25b Image 3): Filter the suspension; sand is retained as residue on filter paper.
4. Step 4 (Evaporation - Fig. 5.25b Image 2): Heat the clear salt filtrate to evaporate water and collect dry common salt crystals.

essay.q: Explain the principle and technique of crystallization for purifying solid substances, and describe the role of cooling rate on crystal size.
essay.a:
1. Principle: Relies on the decrease in solubility of solid solutes in a liquid solvent as temperature drops. When a hot saturated solution cools, excess solute precipitates out as pure geometric crystals, while impurities remain in solution.
2. Procedure: Dissolve the impure solid in minimum hot water to form a saturated solution, filter hot to remove insoluble impurities, and allow the clear filtrate to cool undisturbed.
3. Effect of Cooling Rate:
- Slow Cooling (Room Temperature): Low supersaturation gives solute particles ample time to assemble systematically into orderly repeating lattices, producing large, well-defined, shiny crystals.
- Rapid Cooling (Ice Bath): High supersaturation causes sudden, chaotic nucleation, resulting in numerous small, powdery, poorly-formed crystals.
4. Application: Purification of copper sulfate (CuSO₄) and commercial manufacturing of sugar crystals (mishri).

essay.q: Differentiate between simple distillation and fractional distillation with respect to their working principles, apparatus setups, and industrial applications.
essay.a:
1. Simple Distillation:
- Principle: Separates miscible liquids with a boiling point difference (Δb.p.) of at least 25 °C, or a volatile liquid from a non-volatile solid.
- Apparatus: Distillation flask, thermometer, Liebig water condenser, and receiver flask.
- Application: Separating acetone (56 °C) and water (100 °C); obtaining pure drinking water from salt water.

2. Fractional Distillation:
- Principle: Separates miscible liquids whose boiling points differ by less than 25 °C (Δb.p. < 25 °C).
- Apparatus: Employs a fractionating column packed with glass beads placed between the flask and condenser, providing multiple continuous condensation-vaporization cycles.
- Application: Refining crude petroleum into fractions (LPG, petrol, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, bitumen); separating atmospheric gases.

essay.q: Describe the principle and procedure for separating two immiscible liquids using a separating funnel, taking cooking oil and water as an example.
essay.a:
1. Principle: Immiscible liquids do not dissolve in each other and separate into distinct horizontal layers based on their densities.
2. Procedure:
- Pour the mixture of cooking oil and water into a separating funnel supported on a retort stand.
- Allow the mixture to stand undisturbed for several minutes.
- Cooking oil (density 0.91 g/mL) floats to form the upper layer, while denser water (density 1.00 g/mL) settles as the lower layer.
- Open the stopcock at the bottom to drain the lower water layer into a receiving beaker.
- Close the stopcock precisely as the oil-water interface reaches the bore, leaving the oil in the funnel.
3. Application: Separating oil spills from water; solvent extraction of organic compounds in pharmaceutical manufacturing.

essay.q: Explain the process of sublimation as a separation technique, and describe how a mixture of camphor and sand is separated in the laboratory.
essay.a:
1. Principle: Sublimation is the direct phase transition of a substance from solid to gas on heating without passing through the liquid phase (reverse is deposition). It separates a sublimable solid from a non-sublimable solid.
2. Laboratory Procedure:
- Place the crushed camphor and sand mixture in a china dish.
- Cover the dish with an inverted glass funnel, plugging its stem with cotton to prevent vapours from escaping.
- Heat gently over a burner. Camphor sublimes into vapour, rises, and contacts the cooler inner walls of the funnel, undergoing deposition into pure white solid crystals.
- Non-sublimable sand remains behind in the dish.
3. Other Sublimable Substances: Naphthalene, ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl), iodine crystals, and dry ice (solid CO₂).

essay.q: Based on Activity 5.1, compare a true solution (salt in water), a suspension (chalk in water), and a colloid (milk in water) across particle size, visibility, Tyndall effect, stability, and filterability.
essay.a:
1. True Solution (Salt in water):
- Particle size: < 1 nm; invisible to the naked eye.
- Laser beam (Tyndall effect): Not visible (no scattering).
- Stability: Completely stable; particles never settle.
- Filterability: Passes completely through filter paper without residue.

2. Suspension (Chalk in water):
- Particle size: > 1000 nm; visible to the naked eye.
- Laser beam: Visible due to scattering by suspended particles.
- Stability: Unstable; particles settle to the bottom on standing.
- Filterability: Chalk particles are retained on filter paper as residue.

3. Colloid (Milk in water):
- Particle size: 1–1000 nm; individual particles invisible.
- Laser beam: Distinctly visible (exhibits Tyndall scattering).
- Stability: Stable; particles remain dispersed without settling.
- Filterability: Passes through filter paper without residue.

essay.q: State the mathematical formulas and practical applications for the three common percentage methods used to express solution concentration.
essay.a:
1. Mass by Mass Percentage (% m/m):
- Formula: [Mass of solute / Mass of solution] × 100
  where Mass of solution = Mass of solute + Mass of solvent.
- Example: 10 g salt in 90 g water = (10 / 100) × 100 = 10% m/m.
- Application: Nutrition labels, dry powder blends, alloys.

2. Mass by Volume Percentage (% m/v):
- Formula: [Mass of solute (g) / Volume of solution (mL)] × 100
- Example: Standard hospital IV saline is 0.9% m/v NaCl (0.9 g NaCl per 100 mL solution).
- Application: Clinical medicine, pharmaceutical syrups, lab reagents.

3. Volume by Volume Percentage (% v/v):
- Formula: [Volume of solute (mL) / Volume of solution (mL)] × 100
- Example: Commercial vinegar contains 5% v/v acetic acid (5 mL acetic acid per 100 mL solution).
- Application: Miscible liquid mixtures, perfumes, alcoholic beverages.

essay.q: Describe the step-by-step laboratory method for preparing pure crystals of copper sulfate (blue vitriol) from an impure sample (Activity 5.3), stating key precautions.
essay.a:
1. Procedure:
- Dissolve 1 g of copper sulfate in 25 mL of water in a beaker.
- Add 1 drop of dilute sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) to prevent hydrolysis of copper sulfate.
- Heat gently in a water bath while stirring continuously.
- Add more copper sulfate powder until no more dissolves, preparing a hot saturated solution.
- Filter hot through a funnel with filter paper to remove insoluble impurities.
- Cover the clear blue filtrate with a watch glass and allow it to cool slowly and undisturbed at room temperature.
- Filter, rinse with cold water, and dry the large shiny blue crystals formed.
2. Key Precautions:
- Copper sulfate is toxic; avoid skin contact and do not ingest.
- Keep the solution completely undisturbed during cooling to ensure well-formed crystals.

essay.q: Explain India's traditional heritage in distillation with reference to the Deg-Bhapka perfumery technique of Kannauj and the creation of Mitti ka Ittar.
essay.a:
1. Kannauj - Perfume Capital of India: Renowned for centuries in Uttar Pradesh for traditional hydro-distillation of natural perfumes (ittars).
2. Deg-Bhapka Apparatus & Operation:
- Deg (Still): Copper cauldron loaded with flower petals or clay and water, sealed with mud and rope, and heated over firewood.
- Chonga: Hollow bamboo pipe that channels fragrant steam from the deg to the receiver.
- Bhapka (Receiver): Copper vessel filled with base sandalwood oil, immersed in a cold water tank that acts as a natural condenser.
3. Mitti ka Ittar: Made by distilling sun-baked clay cakes, capturing the earthy aroma of dry soil after the first monsoon rain (petrichor).
4. Modern Support: Fragrance and Flavour Development Centre (FFDC) provides technical support and quality testing.

essay.q: Explain the principle of centrifugation, give two everyday examples, and describe how the Paperfuge helps in rural medical diagnostics.
essay.a:
1. Principle: Rapid rotational spinning produces centrifugal force that drives denser suspended particles outward to the bottom of the container, leaving lighter liquid as supernatant.
2. Everyday Examples: Dairies separating cream and butter from milk; domestic washing machines spinning clothes dry.
3. The Paperfuge (Social Innovation):
- Device: A low-cost, electricity-free hand-powered centrifuge inspired by the whirligig toy, made from a paper disc and braided twine.
- Performance: Pulling the strings spins capillary blood tubes at over 100,000 rpm.
- Significance: Separates blood plasma from red blood cells in under 90 seconds, enabling diagnostic detection of malaria and anaemia in remote non-electrified clinics.

essay.q: Explain the scientific mechanism of coagulation using alum (fitkari) to clarify turbid water, and contrast it with filtration.
essay.a:
1. Mechanism of Coagulation:
- Muddy water contains microscopic colloidal clay particles that carry like negative electrical charges, causing mutual repulsion and preventing them from settling.
- Added powdered alum releases trivalent aluminium ions (Al³⁺) that neutralize these negative surface charges.
- Neutralized particles collide and clump together into larger, heavier aggregates called flocs (coagulation).
- These heavy flocs settle quickly to the bottom by gravity (sedimentation), allowing clear water to be decanted.
2. Contrast with Filtration:
- Filtration physically blocks particles larger than paper pores. Fine colloidal clay passes straight through filter paper unless first coagulated into larger flocs.

essay.q: Using the solubility data from Table 5.4, (i) calculate the mass of KNO₃ needed for 50 g water at 40 °C, (ii) describe what happens when saturated KCl at 80 °C cools to 25 °C, and (iii) compare temperature effects on KNO₃ vs NaCl.
essay.a:
1. Part (i) KNO₃ at 40 °C:
- Solubility from Table 5.4 = 62 g per 100 g of water.
- Mass required for 50 g of water = (62 / 100) × 50 = 31 g.

2. Part (ii) Cooling saturated KCl from 80 °C to 25 °C:
- At 80 °C, 100 g water dissolves 54 g KCl. At 25 °C, it dissolves ~36 g KCl.
- Observation: Glistening solid crystals of KCl precipitate out and deposit at the bottom.
- Reason: As temperature decreases, solubility drops, forcing the excess ~18 g solute to crystallize.

3. Part (iii) Comparison of Temperature Effects:
- KNO₃: Surges from 21 g at 10 °C to 167 g at 80 °C (+146 g, +695%), showing highest temperature sensitivity.
- NaCl: Increases only from 36 g at 10 °C to 37 g at 80 °C (+1 g, +2.8%), showing an almost flat solubility curve.

essay.q: Three students prepare sugar solutions: Student A (20 g sugar in 80 g water), Student B (20 g sugar in 100 g water), and Student C (30 g sugar in 80 g water). Calculate each % m/m concentration and identify the most concentrated.
essay.a:
Formula: Mass % (% m/m) = [Mass of solute / (Mass of solute + Mass of solvent)] × 100

1. Student A:
- Mass of solute = 20 g, Mass of solution = 20 + 80 = 100 g.
- % m/m = (20 / 100) × 100 = 20.00% m/m.

2. Student B:
- Mass of solute = 20 g, Mass of solution = 20 + 100 = 120 g.
- % m/m = (20 / 120) × 100 ≈ 16.67% m/m.

3. Student C:
- Mass of solute = 30 g, Mass of solution = 30 + 80 = 110 g.
- % m/m = (30 / 110) × 100 ≈ 27.27% m/m.

4. Conclusion: Student C's solution is the most concentrated (27.27% m/m) because it contains the highest proportion of solute in the total solution mass.

essay.q: In Fig. 5.26, identify technique S, label apparatus A, B, and C, and explain which mixtures from Table 5.5 can be separated by this setup.
essay.a:
1. Identification: Technique S is Simple Distillation.
2. Labels:
- A: Distillation flask (round-bottom flask fitted with thermometer).
- B: Liebig water condenser (cool water enters lower inlet, exits upper outlet).
- C: Conical flask (receiver for collecting liquid distillate).
3. Feasibility of Mixtures (Criterion: Δb.p. ≥ 25 °C or liquid from non-volatile solid):
- (a) Water (100 °C) - Acetone (56 °C): Δ = 44 °C (≥ 25 °C) -> Separated by simple distillation.
- (b) Water - Salt: Volatile liquid and non-volatile solid -> Separated by simple distillation.
- (c) Acetone (56 °C) - Alcohol (78 °C): Δ = 22 °C (< 25 °C) -> Not separated (requires fractional distillation).
- (d) Sand - Salt: Both non-volatile solids -> Not separated by distillation.
- (e) Alcohol (78 °C) - Chloroform (61 °C): Δ = 17 °C (< 25 °C) -> Not separated.
- (f) Alcohol (78 °C) - Benzene (80 °C): Δ = 2 °C (< 25 °C) -> Not separated.
Conclusion: Only mixtures (a) and (b) can be separated by this setup.

essay.q: Outline the step-by-step separation sequence for a mixture of sand, common salt, and naphthalene, correlating each step with the images in Fig. 5.25b.
essay.a:
1. Step 1 (Sublimation - Fig. 5.25b Image 1):
- Heat the solid mixture in a china dish covered with an inverted cotton-plugged funnel.
- Naphthalene sublimes directly into vapour and deposits on the cooler funnel walls as pure crystals.
- Sand and common salt remain behind in the dish.
2. Step 2 (Dissolution):
- Add water to the residual sand-salt mixture and stir well.
- Common salt dissolves completely in water; sand remains undissolved.
3. Step 3 (Filtration - Fig. 5.25b Image 3):
- Pour through a funnel fitted with filter paper.
- Insoluble sand is retained as residue on the filter paper, washed, and dried.
- Clear sodium chloride solution passes through as filtrate.
4. Step 4 (Evaporation - Fig. 5.25b Image 2):
- Heat the salt filtrate in an evaporating dish to boil off water.
- Dry crystals of common salt are obtained.
5. Correct Image Sequence: Image 1 -> Image 3 -> Image 2.
